memory_update.text: AI should be tracked as a multi-node infrastructure buildout: accelerators, memory, advanced packaging, networking, power, cooling, grid, and automation software rather than a single semiconductor theme.
HBM/advanced-packaging research must separate HBM stack process exposure from FC-BGA/ABF substrate exposure; the two flows have different demand drivers and bottlenecks.

ABF substrate materials and surface chemistry are high-priority underfollowed lanes because provided evidence indicates very high supplier concentration in insulating film and copper-bonding chemistry.
AI-server MLCCs and upstream barium titanate dielectric powders are a promising second-order lane with potential small/mid-cap discovery outside obvious GPU and HBM names.

Compound-semiconductor epitaxy tools for optical interconnect are a high-quality research lane because AI networking demand can propagate upstream from transceivers to lasers, wafers, epitaxy, and deposition equipment.
Layer 1B should add primary-source verification, current market-cap screens, analyst-coverage checks, and candidate universes across Japan, Taiwan, Korea, Europe, and U.S. markets.

Software and automation remain underdeveloped in this Layer 1A because the supplied evidence is stronger for physical AI infrastructure; a separate branch should screen niche vertical AI, data-governance, test-automation, and industrial workflow software.

summary: Layer 1A decomposes AI as a physical infrastructure and automation theme rather than a single GPU trade. The highest-quality discovery lanes are one or two layers beneath obvious AI leaders: HBM/advanced-packaging materials, substrate chemistry, optical/compound-semiconductor epitaxy tools, AI-server power passives, upstream MLCC powders, and data-center power/cooling/grid execution. Reference leaders such as NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, TSMC, ASML, Arista, Vertiv, Eaton, hyperscalers, and major utilities remain useful as demand validators, but the Serenity funnel should hunt for smaller or less-followed suppliers whose products are hard to qualify, capacity-constrained, or embedded in customer supply chains. This is research support only and does not provide buy/sell recommendations.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: The chokepoint is not only HBM producer wafer capacity; it may also be stack yield, bonding/underfill process control, inspection throughput, and advanced-packaging integration capacity.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Prefer USD 300M-10B process-equipment or materials names; include larger semi-equipment companies only as reference anchors if their HBM exposure is too diluted.
supply_chain_nodes.node: HBM stack process and advanced-packaging workflow: die thinning, vertical interconnects, bonding, underfill, inspection, and co-packaging with accelerators
supply_chain_nodes.public_asset_hunting_notes: Map public suppliers of temporary bonding/debonding, wafer thinning, TSV/metrology, underfill, bonding tools, inspection, substrate attachment, and OSAT/advanced-packaging capacity. Separate direct HBM-stack exposure from general advanced-packaging exposure.
supply_chain_nodes.underfollowed_angle: The provided HBM source warns that investors often conflate the HBM stack flow and substrate flow. A better discovery lane is companies with cleaner exposure to the HBM stack process, especially smaller tool/material suppliers with limited analyst focus.
supply_chain_nodes.why_it_matters: AI accelerator performance increasingly depends on HBM bandwidth and advanced packaging capacity, not just logic GPU availability. This node links AI demand to process steps that may scale more slowly than end-market orders.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: The highest-control points may sit beneath substrate makers: insulating film, surface-treatment chemistry, and yield-critical substrate process materials. These suppliers may capture value regardless of which substrate maker wins a specific accelerator socket.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Look for Japan/Taiwan/Korea listed specialty-chemical or substrate suppliers in USD 300M-10B range; larger companies can be tracked if the segment has exceptional strategic relevance.
supply_chain_nodes.node: FC-BGA / ABF package substrate materials and copper-bonding surface chemistry
supply_chain_nodes.public_asset_hunting_notes: Start with ABF film, copper adhesion/surface chemistry, substrate makers, and process-chemical suppliers. Verify revenue exposure to AI/HPC substrate demand and whether products are sole/near-sole sourced.
supply_chain_nodes.underfollowed_angle: The market may know Ibiden and Unimicron as substrate makers, but thinner coverage may exist in suppliers of insulating film and copper-bonding chemistry. However, some controlling assets may be embedded in larger companies or not pure-play investable.
supply_chain_nodes.why_it_matters: AI accelerators require complex package substrates that connect logic dies and HBM stacks. The provided evidence says the substrate constraint is yield rather than simple throughput, which makes materials and process chemistry potentially powerful bottlenecks.

supply_chain_nodes.bottleneck_hypothesis: The most underappreciated bottleneck may be compound-semiconductor epitaxy capacity and the specialized deposition tools used to grow precise optical materials, rather than the visible optical-module vendors alone.
supply_chain_nodes.market_cap_hunting_notes: Target USD 1B-15B compound semi equipment, photonics component, wafer, epi, and testing names; classify >USD 15B optical leaders as reference unless exposure is unusually pure.
supply_chain_nodes.node: Optical interconnect and compound-semiconductor epitaxy tool chain: lasers, photonics, InP/GaAs epitaxy, and MOCVD/deposition tools
supply_chain_nodes.public_asset_hunting_notes: Map 800G/1.6T optical-module vendors, laser suppliers, InP/GaAs wafer and epi suppliers, MOCVD/deposition equipment makers, and metrology suppliers. Verify whether AI-related optical demand is material to revenue rather than a loose narrative.

demand_drivers: Fact: Hyperscaler AI capex and accelerator deployments drive demand for GPUs/ASICs, HBM, advanced packaging, networking, power delivery, cooling, and electricity; the provided pilot universe includes NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, TSMC, Arista, Vertiv, Eaton, Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, and Meta as reference demand validators.

Inference: Scaling from AI training clusters to inference factories increases the importance of networking, optical interconnect, power integrity, thermal density, and data-center electrical infrastructure.

Hypothesis: As the market becomes more efficient at pricing obvious AI leaders, incremental research alpha shifts toward hard-to-expand upstream materials, tools, qualification-constrained components, and second-order power/grid beneficiaries.

Hypothesis: AI software and automation demand will eventually separate into application-layer winners, data-governance platforms, workflow automation vendors, and vertical industrial software; however, Layer 1A prioritizes the physical bottlenecks because evidence in the provided context is stronger there.

theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Run a two-lane funnel. Lane 1 maps reference leaders to confirm demand: accelerators, HBM, foundry, networking, hyperscaler capex, data-center power/cooling, grid and utility constraints. Lane 2 hunts for underfollowed public companies below the obvious leaders: substrate materials, copper/ABF chemistry, HBM stack process equipment, MLCC makers and powder suppliers, optical laser/epi tool suppliers, electrical protection/switchgear subcomponents, thermal-fluid components, testing/inspection, and niche software/data-automation vendors. For Layer 1B, screen public companies with market caps roughly USD 300M-10B where possible, USD 10B-30B only for unusually pure exposure, and micro-caps only as speculative shadow candidates. Evidence should prioritize annual reports, investor presentations, customer disclosures, patent/technical docs, capex guidance, capacity expansion filings, and segment revenue changes.
